title: Bengaluru Eateries Raise Prices 10-15% as Rice, Milk and LPG Costs Surge
excerpt: Tea and coffee are up Rs 3-5 and a Rs 100 dosa now costs Rs 110-115 at some hotels, as the hoteliers' association says rice jumped from Rs 65 to Rs 95 a kilo in a month.
body:
• Bengaluru hotels and restaurants have raised food and beverage prices by 10-15%, the Bruhat Bengaluru Hoteliers Association says, after sharp increases in rice, milk, pulses and other input costs.
  • Tea and coffee are up an average of Rs 3-5; a dosa that cost about Rs 100 now runs about Rs 110-115 at some establishments.
  • Association president P.C. Rao said rice has risen from Rs 65 per kg to as much as Rs 95 per kg in the past month.
  • It is the second round of restaurant price increases this year, landing just before Diwali — and eateries in Mumbai and Pune are weighing similar hikes.

Eating out in Bengaluru just got more expensive. Hotels and restaurants across the city have raised prices on food and beverages by 10-15% after a sharp run-up in the cost of rice, milk, pulses and other raw materials, according to reporting by Urban Acres. Tea and coffee prices have risen by an average of Rs 3-5, and staples such as idli and dosa — the breakfast backbone of the city's darshini restaurants — have gone up with everything else.

The arithmetic behind the hike

P.C. Rao of the Bruhat Bengaluru Hoteliers Association said the price of rice had increased from Rs 65 per kg to as much as Rs 95 per kg over the past month, and that many restaurants had little choice but to pass part of the higher input costs on to customers. A dosa that previously cost around Rs 100 is now priced at about Rs 110-115 at some establishments. The pressure is not only from ingredients: restaurant owners in major cities cite costlier milk and curd, more expensive commercial LPG, food inflation and higher staff salaries, Hind First reported.

Not just Bengaluru, and not the first time this year

Owners in Mumbai and Pune are preparing similar increases of 10-15%, and if the hikes go through nationally it will mark the second time this year that restaurant prices have risen — this round landing in the middle of the festive season, when dining out and ordering in both peak. The increases apply to online orders as well as dining in, so the higher bill follows customers home. Karnataka's hotels had already been squeezed by the state government's Rs 8-per-litre increase in Nandini milk prices, which the hoteliers' association said would force up the price of every milk-based item on the menu, from filter coffee to curd.

What it means at the table

For Bengaluru's office workers and students, who rely on affordable hotels and darshinis for daily meals, a 10-15% rise is not abstract: it is Rs 3-5 more on every coffee, roughly Rs 10-15 more on a dosa, repeated two or three times a day. Restaurants say they have capped the pass-through below the full rise in their costs to avoid straining customers further. Whether that holds depends on whether rice and milk prices stabilise — Rao's figures suggest input costs rose far faster than menu prices did.
